stations.live: Stop straining to give yourself a new birth. Pray: “Spirit of God, you gave me life. Grow it in me today.”

stations.verse: But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared, not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit…
stations.question: Where am I still trying to earn a washing that God gave me by mercy?
stations.gloss: new birth, renewal, regeneration
body: Palingenesia joins two ideas: again and birth. It appears only twice. Jesus uses it for the renewal of all things when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his glory (Matthew 19:28). Paul uses it for what happened to you: he saved you through the washing of regeneration. The same word stretches from your new birth to the renewal of the world. What God began in you, he will finish in everything.
stations.live: Read Titus 3:4–5 aloud and underline “not by works.” Thank God for one mercy you could never have earned.

practices.title: NAME THE “THIS IS JUST WHO I AM” LIE
practices.body: Most men have an area where they have quietly surrendered to the old self: “I’ll always have this temper.” “I’ll never beat this.” “This is just who I am.” This week, name yours. Write it down. Then write across it the truth from 2 Corinthians 5: in Christ, the old has passed away; behold, the new has come. Naming the resignation is the first step to refusing it. You are not stuck being the man you have always been.

practices.title: GET DRESSED IN THE NEW SELF
practices.body: Paul speaks of putting off the old self and putting on the new like changing clothes. This week, make it a conscious morning act. Before the day starts, “put on” the new self out loud: “In Christ I am a new creation. I am not the old man today. I am God’s workmanship, made new.” You are not pretending; you are agreeing with what God already did, and choosing which self to wear into the day.

practices.title: BRING THE OLD PATTERNS TO THE SON
practices.body: You will be tempted to beat your old patterns by sheer effort and then despair when they resurface. Reverse it. The old self was crucified with Christ, so bring the pattern to him: “Lord, this old habit feels like me, but you put that man to death. I am not obligated to obey a corpse. Live your new life in me here.” When the old pattern whispers, “This is who you are,” answer it: that man passed away in Christ.

practices.title: LET THE SPIRIT DO THE RENEWING
practices.body: The new self is being renewed by the Spirit, not by your striving. This week, instead of white-knuckling change, ask the Spirit to do his creative work: “Holy Spirit, you gave me new birth. Renew me today after the image of my Creator. Grow the new man you already made.” Then cooperate with the renewal instead of trying to manufacture it.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER WHO YOU ARE NOW
practices.body: The dust keeps a man anchored to his old reputation, especially his reputation with himself. Before the week ends, tell a trusted brother the old identity you are putting off and the new one you are putting on, and ask him to call you by the new name when you forget. New identities are reinforced in community and eroded in isolation.

title: A New Creation
subtitle: from dust to new birth
keyVerse: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.

passage.text: For the love of Christ constrains us; because we judge thus, that one died for all, therefore all died.
He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.
Therefore we know no one after the flesh from now on. Even though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now we know him so no more.
Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first. Then answer the question honestly, and let the word study sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeIntro: This week is not about feeling brand new by Friday. It is about living from a new creation God already made. Here is how that lands in real life, with the Father, the Son, and the Spirit woven through.
lifePulls: Willpower can only polish the old man. It cannot create a new one. But in Christ, God already has.
prayer: Father, I have made peace with the old man more often than I want to admit. I confess I say “this is just who I am” as if you had not spoken. Thank you that in Christ I am a new creation. Thank you for the washing of regeneration I did nothing to earn. Clothe me in the new man today. Finish the work you are making in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I have made peace with the old man more often than I want to admit. I confess I say “this is just
who I am” as if you had not spoken. Thank you that in Christ I am a new creation. Thank you for the
washing of regeneration I did nothing to earn. Clothe me in the new man today. Finish the work you are
making in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old things have passed away. You are not renovating the old man. God made a new one, and you are learning to put him on.
benediction: Brother, the dust will keep insisting that you are stuck — that the man you have always been is the man you will always be, that change is a door that closed long ago. Lift your eyes off that lie and onto the God who makes new things. The same God who spoke light out of darkness, who called a universe into being out of nothing, reached into your life and made you a new creation in Christ. He did not improve the old man. He crucified him with Christ and raised a new man in his place. The old has passed away. Behold — look up and see it — the new has come.

So when the old patterns resurface this week and the dust says nothing has really changed, lift up your eyes. When you fail in the old familiar way and want to surrender to “this is just who I am,” lift up your eyes. When change feels impossible, lift up your eyes to the One for whom new creation is no trouble at all. Jesus took on flesh and died your death so that the old you could die with him, and he rose so that a new you could rise with him. You were born again, not of your own effort, but of the Spirit, to a living hope that does not disappoint.

This is from dust to revival — not a man renovating his old self, but a man lifting his eyes to the new self God already created in Christ. You are not the old man limping along. You are God’s workmanship, his new creation, his made-new son, and the life you live now is the unfolding of what he already made. Lift up your eyes to the Creator who made you new, and walk as the new man you already are. Behold, the new has come. Welcome to week five of living in it.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust of the old self, but in Christ the old has passed away and the new has come. Lift up your eyes and live new.
carry: Which old habit have you been calling your identity instead of your former way of life?

sections.heading: The Distance the Dust Keeps
pulls: You are not a forgiven stranger kept at the door. In Christ you have been brought near and welcomed to the table.
paras: The dust does more than make a man feel guilty; it makes him feel far away. Even after he believes he is forgiven, something in him keeps God at arm’s length — approaches cautiously, prays from a distance, half-expects a cold reception. He relates to God the way a man relates to someone he has wronged badly: technically reconciled, perhaps, but the warmth is gone, the ease is gone, and he would rather not get too close in case the old offense is still hanging in the air. He lives like a man permitted back into the house but no longer welcome at the table.

Into that careful distance Paul speaks the word reconciliation. While you were an enemy, he says, you were reconciled to God through the death of his Son. The hostility is over — not managed, not paused, but ended. And reconciliation is not only the end of hostility; it is the return of warmth. Paul says you now have peace with God, that you who once were far off have been made near, that you have access to the Father. The man in Christ is not tolerated at a wary distance. He has been brought all the way near and welcomed to the table.

sections.heading: The Hostility Is Over From Both Sides
paras: Reconciliation means the enmity is gone in both directions. From God’s side, the wrath your sin deserved fell on Christ, so there is nothing left in God toward you but welcome. From your side, the hostility and fear and self-protection that kept you running from God are answered, because the cross removes every reason to hide. Paul says God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them. Not counting. The ledger that kept the distance has been cleared, and with it the reason for the distance.

This is why the man in Christ can come close. He is not gambling that God might be in a good mood. He is resting on a peace that was made at the cross, a reconciliation finished while he was still hostile to God. The dust will keep urging him to hang back, to approach God carefully, to assume a cold reception. The Word urges him to come near, because the hostility is over and the Father is waiting.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Hostility Is Over
paras: Paul uses startling language: you were an enemy, and you were reconciled. He does not soften the before-picture. Apart from Christ, a man is not merely distant from God; he is at odds with him, alienated and hostile in mind. But the cross did not just narrow the gap — it ended the hostility. To be reconciled is to have the enmity removed and the relationship restored. And notice when it happened: while you were still an enemy. God did not wait for you to turn around and come crawling back before he made peace. He made peace through the death of his Son while you were still in rebellion, and then he came and found you.

This means your peace with God does not depend on your keeping the peace. It rests on peace made through the blood of Christ, accomplished before you did anything to deserve it. The dust says the hostility could flare up again with your next failure. The Word says the hostility is over, ended by Another, and your failures arrive too late to reopen what the cross already settled.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Brought Near by the Blood
paras: Paul tells the Ephesians that they who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. Far off is the language of exclusion — outsiders, strangers, those with no access. Brought near is the language of belonging — insiders, family, those welcomed in. And the means is the blood. The same blood that ransomed you and justified you also closes the distance, bringing the far-off man all the way into the presence of God. Christ himself, Paul says, is the peace of his people, the One who broke down the middle wall of separation.

So when you feel far off this week — and the dust will work hard to make you feel it — the answer is not to try to inch closer by your own effort, as if you could earn back the nearness. The answer is to believe the nearness the blood already purchased. You have been brought near. The distance you feel is not the distance you are at. In Christ, you are near.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Access, Not Just Amnesty
paras: Reconciliation gives more than a cleared record; it gives access. Paul says that through Christ both Jew and Gentile have access in one Spirit to the Father, and that through him you have access by faith into this grace in which you stand. The writer of Hebrews presses it further: you have boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus, and you are invited to draw near with boldness to the throne of grace. The reconciled man is not granted amnesty and then sent away. He is granted entrance — the right to come close, to draw near, to approach the throne not as a trembling outsider but as a welcomed son.

This is the warmth the dust keeps stealing. A man can believe he is forgiven and still never draw near, still keep the relationship cold and cautious. But reconciliation invites him to the table. The throne of grace is open, the access is purchased, and the Father is not bracing for the visit — he is waiting for it. The call is not merely to be at peace with God from a distance, but to come close and enjoy the nearness that peace makes possible.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to the Table
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the far country: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). And the reviving word for a man who keeps his distance is reconciliation. You are not a forgiven stranger lingering at the door. In Christ the hostility is over, the distance is closed, and you have been brought near and given access to the Father. Revival, for a man who relates to God from arm’s length, begins the moment he believes the nearness the blood purchased and actually comes close — to the table, to the throne of grace, to the Father who has been waiting.

So this week, when the dust urges you to hang back and approach God carefully, lift your eyes to what Christ accomplished. The hostility is gone. The distance is closed. You have been brought near by his blood. You are not a man hoping to be readmitted. You are a reconciled son with full access, invited to draw near with confidence to a Father who reconciled you while you were still his enemy and now welcomes you all the way home.

stations.verse: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off are made near in the blood of Christ.
stations.question: I have been made near in the blood of Christ — what would change if I lived this week as a man already close?
stations.gloss: near, close at hand
body: Engys means near. Paul sets it against its opposite: you who once were far off are made near. The distance was real, and you could not close it. Look at what closed it: the blood of Christ. Nearness to God is not something you win by feeling close. It was bought for you, and it holds on the days you feel far away.
stations.live: When you feel far off, do not try to earn your way closer. Say: “I am made near in the blood of Christ.” Then pray as a near man.

stations.verse: For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation…
stations.question: What wall am I still standing behind that Christ has already broken down?
stations.gloss: a dividing wall, a partition
body: Mesotoichon is a partition wall, a wall set between two parties. It appears only here in the New Testament. Paul says Christ is your peace, who made both one and broke down the middle wall of separation. He is writing about Jew and Gentile made one people. The same work tears down the wall between God and you, and between you and the brother you keep at arm’s length.
stations.live: Name one man you have walled off. Before the week ends, take one step toward him — a call, a word, a meal.

stations.verse: For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we will be saved by his life. Not only so, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation.
stations.question: What am I boasting in this week — my record, or God through my Lord Jesus Christ?
stations.gloss: to boast, to glory, to rejoice in
body: Kauchaomai means to boast, to glory in something. Paul warns against boasting in yourself, then turns the word around: “He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31). Here WEB renders it rejoice — you rejoice in God through your Lord Jesus Christ. The reconciled man still has something to boast about. It is just no longer himself.
stations.live: Before bed each night this week, name one thing God did in Christ that day, and thank him for it out loud.

stations.verse: For through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father.
stations.question: Am I using the access I have to the Father, or standing outside a door that is already open?
stations.gloss: access, approach, the way in
body: Prosagōgē is access — the way in, the approach to someone. Paul uses it three times, always of coming to God: access in one Spirit to the Father, access by faith into grace (Romans 5:2), boldness and access in confidence (Ephesians 3:12). Access is not permission you request each morning. It is a way that stays open, because Christ opened it.
stations.live: Pray this week without clearing your throat first. Walk in: “Father, through Jesus, by the Spirit, here I am.”

stations.verse: Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and may find grace for help in time of need.
stations.question: What makes me come to God braced for a courtroom, when he calls it the throne of grace?
stations.gloss: a throne, a seat of rule
body: Thronos is a throne — the seat of a king. A throne is where rule is exercised and judgment is given. Hebrews does not take that away. It names the throne you approach: the throne of grace. The same seat of power is the place where you receive mercy and find help in time of need. You are told to come with boldness, because the one on the throne has already dealt with your sin.
stations.live: Bring one need to God this week that you have been too ashamed to name. Come to the throne of grace, not the courtroom.

practices.title: NAME THE DISTANCE YOU KEEP
practices.body: Most men keep a specific kind of distance from God — praying only when desperate, avoiding him after failure, relating from a careful arm’s length. This week, name yours. When and why do you hang back? Write it down, then write across it the truth from Ephesians 2: brought near by the blood of Christ. You cannot close a distance you will not admit you keep. Name it, and let the Word answer it.

practices.title: DRAW NEAR ON PURPOSE, ESPECIALLY AFTER FAILURE
practices.body: The dust says: after you fail, keep your distance until you feel worthy again. Reverse it. This week, the moment you fail, draw near instead of pulling back — go straight to the throne of grace, because that is precisely where mercy and grace to help are found. Practice approaching God first in your worst moments, not your best. Confident drawing-near, especially after failure, is what reconciliation makes possible.

practices.title: COME TO THE FATHER THROUGH THE SON
practices.body: You will be tempted to try to earn your way back into warmth with God. Reverse it. Your access is through Christ, who is himself your peace. Come to the Father in him: “Father, I come through Jesus, my peace. I will not stand at the door when the blood has brought me near.” When the sense of distance returns this week, answer it: I am near, in Christ, and the access is already mine.

practices.title: LET THE SPIRIT BRING YOU IN
practices.body: Paul says you have access in one Spirit to the Father. When you pray this week and feel far off, ask the Spirit to do what he was given to do: “Holy Spirit, carry me near. Make the access real to me. Help me draw near with boldness to the Father who reconciled me.” Then pray as one already brought in, not one still knocking.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER WHERE YOU HANG BACK
practices.body: The dust isolates a man and then convinces him his distance from God is permanent. Before the week ends, tell a trusted brother where you keep God at arm’s length, and ask him to remind you that you have been brought near. Sometimes a man needs another voice to call him back to the table.

title: Reconciled and Brought Near
subtitle: from dust to the table
keyVerse: Being therefore justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ…

passage.text: Being therefore justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ;
through whom we also have our access by faith into this grace in which we stand. We rejoice in hope of the glory of God.
Not only this, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance;
and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope:
and hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.
For while we were yet weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.
For one will hardly die for a righteous man. Yet perhaps for a righteous person someone would even dare to die.
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we will be saved from God’s wrath through him.
For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we will be saved by his life.
Not only so, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first. Then answer the question honestly, and let the word study sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeIntro: This week is not about feeling close to God by Friday. It is about living from a nearness the blood already purchased. Here is how that lands in real life, with the Father, the Son, and the Spirit woven through.
lifePulls: The dust tells you to approach God carefully, braced for a cold reception. The cross tells you the Father has been waiting at the table.
prayer: Father, I keep you at arm’s length and call it respect. I confess I come to you braced for a cold reception. Thank you that while I was your enemy you reconciled me through the death of your Son. Thank you that I am made near in his blood and have access to you by one Spirit. Bring me all the way in today. Let me come to the throne of grace with boldness. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I keep you at arm’s length and call it respect. I confess I come to you braced for a cold reception.
Thank you that while I was your enemy you reconciled me through the death of your Son. Thank you that
I am made near in his blood and have access to you by one Spirit. Bring me all the way in today. Let me
come to the throne of grace with boldness. In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Romans 5:1 hands a distant man the warmth the dust keeps stealing: being justified by faith, you have peace with God through your Lord Jesus Christ. The hostility is over, the distance is closed, and you have been made near by the blood. You do not have to stand at the door.
benediction: Brother, the dust will always tell you to keep your distance — to approach God carefully, to hang back after you fail, to relate to your Father from across a cold and cautious gap. Lift your eyes off that distance and onto the cross that closed it. While you were still an enemy, God reconciled you to himself through the death of his Son. The hostility is over. The wrath your sin deserved fell on Christ, and now there is nothing left in the Father toward you but welcome. You who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ, and he himself is your peace.

So when you feel far away this week, lift up your eyes. When you fail and your instinct is to pull back, lift up your eyes and draw near instead. When you approach God braced for a cold reception, lift up your eyes to the Father who has been waiting at the table the whole time. Jesus took on flesh and bore the hostility your sin had earned, breaking down the dividing wall, opening the way into the holy place by his own blood, so that you could come near with confidence and find mercy and grace in your time of need.

This is from dust to revival — not a man earning his way back into warmth, but a man lifting his eyes and walking into a nearness already purchased. You are not a forgiven stranger lingering at the door. You are a reconciled son with full access, invited to draw near to a Father who reconciled you while you were still an enemy and now welcomes you home. Lift up your eyes to your peace, and come to the table. Welcome to week six of living near.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust of the far country, but in Christ you have been brought near. Lift up your eyes — the Father is at the table.
carry: What distance are you keeping from the Father that the blood of Christ has already closed?

sections.heading: The Fear of Slipping Through the Cracks
pulls: You are not holding onto God by a grip that might slip. You have been sealed by God, and his Spirit is the pledge.
paras: There is a quiet fear that follows many a Christian man into the dust: the fear that he could still be lost. Not lost through some dramatic rejection, but simply slipping through the cracks — falling one too many times, drifting one degree too far, waking up one day outside the grace he thought he was inside. He believes he is saved, mostly, but he holds it nervously, the way a man holds something he is afraid he might drop. And so he never quite rests, because the whole weight of staying saved feels like it rests on his ability to hold on.

Into that nervous grip Paul speaks two words from the world of commerce and ownership: sealed and pledge. In Christ, he says, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is a pledge of your inheritance. You did not just receive forgiveness; you were stamped with a seal that marks you as God’s own, and God placed his Spirit in you as the down payment on everything still to come. The man in Christ is not holding onto God by a slipping grip. He has been sealed by God, and the Spirit in him is heaven’s pledge that the rest is coming.

sections.heading: Sealed: Marked as Belonging
paras: A seal marks a thing as belonging to someone. To be sealed is to be stamped as the property of one who has the authority to keep you. Paul says God has done exactly this to the man in Christ: he has put his seal on you, marking you as his own possession, authenticating you as genuine, and pledging his protection over you. The seal is not your white-knuckled commitment to God. It is God’s own mark of ownership on you.

And the seal is the Holy Spirit himself. God did not stamp you with an external mark you might lose. He sealed you with his own Spirit, placed inside you, an indwelling pledge that you belong to him. This is why your security does not finally depend on the strength of your grip. The seal was set by God, and a seal pressed by the King is not broken by the trembling of the one who bears it.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Sealed: Marked as God’s Own
paras: Paul says you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit. Stop and consider who did the sealing. You did not seal yourself; God sealed you. The mark of ownership on your life is not your achievement but his action. And what he marks as his own, he keeps. Paul tells the Ephesians not to grieve the Holy Spirit, by whom they were sealed for the day of redemption — meaning the seal holds all the way to the end, all the way to the day your salvation is brought to completion. The seal is not a temporary stamp that fades with your failures. It is set for the day of redemption, and it lasts until that day arrives.

This is the answer to the fear of slipping through the cracks. A sealed man does not slip through; the seal holds him. The dust will tell you that you could still be lost, that your grip is too weak, that one more failure could undo it all. The Word answers that you were sealed by God himself, marked as his own, kept by his Spirit for the day of redemption. Your security rests on his seal, not your strength.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The Pledge, the Down Payment
paras: Paul calls the Spirit a pledge of your inheritance. The word he uses was a commercial term: the first installment, the down payment, the deposit that guarantees the full amount will follow. When a buyer put down a deposit, he was pledging the rest — the down payment was both a real portion of the purchase and a binding promise of the whole. Paul says God has given you his Spirit as exactly that: a real foretaste of the inheritance now, and a binding pledge that the full inheritance is coming. The Spirit in you is heaven’s deposit, God’s own pledge that he will pay in full.

This means the life of the Spirit you experience now is not the whole of your inheritance; it is the down payment on it. The comfort, the assurance, the foretastes of joy and peace the Spirit gives are not the sum total — they are the first installment, the pledge that there is infinitely more to come. The dust says, “This is all you get, and you might lose even this.” The Word says the Spirit in you is the pledge that the best is not only still ahead but secured.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Sealed for the Day of Redemption
paras: Notice how far the seal reaches: for the day of redemption. The seal is not good for a week, or until your next failure, or for as long as you can keep your spiritual act together. It is set for the day of redemption — the day when your salvation will be completed, your body raised, your inheritance fully possessed. From the moment you believed until the moment you stand glorified, the seal holds. There is no gap in it, no expiration, no clause that voids it if you fail enough times. God sealed you for the whole distance, all the way home.

So when the dust threatens you with the fear of being lost, the question to ask is not “Can my grip hold?” but “Will God’s seal hold?” And the answer is settled. The seal is his, set for the day of redemption, and what God seals, God keeps. You are not nervously hanging on, hoping to make it. You are sealed, guaranteed, kept by the Spirit of God for a day that is certain to come.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to Security
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the nervous low place: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). And the reviving word for a man afraid of being lost is sealed. You are not holding onto God by a grip that might fail. In Christ you have been sealed with the Holy Spirit, marked as God’s own possession, given the Spirit as the pledge of an inheritance that is certainly coming. Revival, for a man who never quite rests in his salvation, begins the moment he stops trusting his grip and starts trusting God’s seal.

So this week, when the fear of slipping through the cracks rises, lift your eyes to the seal God set on you. You were stamped as his own. His Spirit lives in you as the down payment on everything still to come. You are not a man nervously trying to stay saved. You are a sealed man, guaranteed, kept by the Spirit of the living God for the day of redemption that is surely on its way.

stations.verse: In him you also, having heard the word of the truth, the Good News of your salvation—in whom, having also believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is a pledge of our inheritance, to the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory.
stations.question: If my salvation ends in the praise of God’s glory, why do I still keep it on my own shoulders?
stations.gloss: praise, approval
body: Epainos is praise. Paul repeats one phrase three times in Ephesians 1: to the praise of the glory of his grace, to the praise of his glory, to the praise of his glory. Your sealing ends there too. God did not seal you so that you could hold yourself together. He sealed you so that, at the end, all of it would bring him praise. A work meant to praise God is not going to fail.
stations.live: When you worry you could slip away, turn the worry into praise. Say: “You sealed me for the praise of your glory.”

stations.verse: Now he who establishes us with you in Christ and anointed us is God, who also sealed us, and gave us the down payment of the Spirit in our hearts.
stations.question: God establishes me, anoints me, seals me — which of those am I still trying to do myself?
stations.gloss: to anoint
body: Chriō means to anoint. The title Christ, the Anointed One, comes from the same root. Jesus read it in the synagogue: the Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me (Luke 4:18). Paul says God has anointed you too, in Christ. The same God establishes you, seals you, and gives the down payment of the Spirit in your heart. Four verbs, one subject. God.
stations.live: Read 2 Corinthians 1:21–22 and circle every verb God does. Then rest in the list.

stations.verse: Now he who made us for this very thing is God, who also gave to us the down payment of the Spirit.
stations.question: God made me for this very thing — do I live like a man with a purpose he designed, or one I have to invent?
stations.gloss: to work out, bring about, prepare fully
body: Katergazomai means to work a thing out to its finish. Paul uses it for light affliction working an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). Here God is the worker: he made you for this very thing — to be clothed with life when what is mortal is swallowed up. He did not start the job and leave you the rest. He gave the down payment of the Spirit to show he means to finish.
stations.live: When the future feels uncertain, remember the down payment. Pray: “You made me for this. You will finish it.”

stations.verse: But if the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised up Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.
stations.question: What fear about my weakening body does the Spirit who raised Jesus answer?
stations.gloss: mortal, subject to death
body: Thnētos means mortal — able to die. Paul does not pretend your body is anything else. But he makes a promise about that mortal body: the Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead will give it life. Elsewhere he says this mortal must put on immortality (1 Corinthians 15:53). The dust your body came from is not where it ends. The Spirit who lives in you now is the pledge of that.
stations.live: The next time your body aches or your age shows, say: “He will give life to my mortal body.”

stations.verse: Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s.
stations.question: I am not my own — how does that change what I do with my body this week?
stations.gloss: to buy, to purchase in the market
body: Agorazō is the market word: to buy. It is used of buying a field, bread, oil. Paul uses it for you: you were bought with a price. Revelation sings the price: “you were killed, and bought us for God with your blood” (Revelation 5:9). Being bought is not only a claim on you. It is security. No one buys at that price to throw away what he bought.
stations.live: Pick one use of your body you have treated as your own business. Hand it over today: “I was bought with a price.”

practices.title: NAME THE FEAR OF BEING LOST
practices.body: Most men carry a specific version of the fear: “One more failure and I’m out.” “I’m barely holding on.” “What if I drift too far?” This week, name yours. Write it down. Then write across it the truth from Ephesians 1: sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, the pledge of the inheritance. You cannot rest until you see that the fear assumes your grip is what holds you — and it never was.

practices.title: TRADE YOUR GRIP FOR HIS SEAL
practices.body: This week, every time the fear rises, consciously hand it over: “I am not holding onto God by my grip. God is holding onto me by his seal. The Spirit in me is his pledge.” Say it until the weight shifts off your strength and onto his. Security is not a feeling you generate; it is a fact you rest on — that God sealed you and keeps you.

practices.title: COME TO THE SON WHO SECURED YOU
practices.body: You will be tempted to secure your salvation by your own diligence and then panic when your diligence falters. Reverse it. Your security is in Christ, who sealed you and gave you his Spirit. Pray it back to him: “Lord, I cannot keep myself. You sealed me. You guaranteed me. I rest in your keeping, not my holding.” When the fear of being lost returns this week, answer it: I am sealed for the day of redemption.

practices.title: RECOGNIZE THE SPIRIT AS YOUR GUARANTEE
practices.body: The Spirit in you is not just power for living; he is the proof and pledge of your inheritance. This week, when you sense any work of the Spirit — a prompting, a comfort, a love for Christ, a hatred of sin — receive it as evidence: “This is the pledge. God put his deposit in me. The rest is certainly coming.” Let the Spirit’s presence be your assurance instead of your performance.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER YOUR INSECURITY
practices.body: The fear of being lost grows in silence. Before the week ends, tell a trusted brother the fear you named, and ask him to remind you that you are sealed and kept. A man who cannot feel his own security sometimes needs a brother to point to the seal he cannot see.

title: Sealed and Guaranteed
subtitle: from dust to security
keyVerse: In him you also, having heard the word of the truth, the Good News of your salvation—in whom, having also believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is a pledge of our inheritance, to the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory.

passage.text: But as God is faithful, our word toward you was not “Yes and no.”
For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, by me, Silvanus, and Timothy, was not “Yes and no,” but in him is “Yes.”
For however many are the promises of God, in him is the “Yes.” Therefore also through him is the “Amen”, to the glory of God through us.
Now he who establishes us with you in Christ and anointed us is God,
who also sealed us, and gave us the down payment of the Spirit in our hearts.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first. Then answer the question honestly, and let the word study sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeIntro: This week is not about feeling secure by Friday. It is about resting in a seal God already set. Here is how that lands in real life, with the Father, the Son, and the Spirit woven through.
lifePulls: The Spirit in you is heaven’s down payment — God’s binding pledge that he will pay the inheritance in full. He does not forfeit his deposits.
prayer: Father, I lie awake afraid I could slip through your fingers. I confess I trust my grip more than your seal. Thank you that you sealed me with the promised Holy Spirit, the pledge of my inheritance. Thank you that I was bought with a price and am not my own. When fear rises today, let me rest in what you have done. Keep me for the day of redemption. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I lie awake afraid I could slip through your fingers. I confess I trust my grip more than your seal.
Thank you that you sealed me with the promised Holy Spirit, the pledge of my inheritance. Thank you
that I was bought with a price and am not my own. When fear rises today, let me rest in what you have
done. Keep me for the day of redemption. In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: In Christ you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, the pledge of your inheritance. Your security was never your grip. It is God’s seal on a man he bought with a price, and he keeps what he seals.
benediction: Brother, the dust will keep whispering that you could still be lost — that your grip is too weak, your failures too many, your hold on God too uncertain to trust. Lift your eyes off your grip and onto God’s seal. The moment you believed, God himself stamped you as his own, sealing you with the promised Holy Spirit and placing within you the down payment of your inheritance. You are not holding onto God by trembling fingers. You have been sealed by the King, and a seal pressed by his hand does not break when yours shakes.

So when the fear of slipping through the cracks rises this week, lift up your eyes. When you fail again and brace for the loss of everything, lift up your eyes. When your hold on God feels too weak to count on, lift up your eyes to the seal that was never your hold in the first place. Jesus secured you, brought you in, and gave you his own Spirit as heaven’s pledge that he will finish what he started. The Spirit in you is God’s binding pledge, and God does not forfeit his deposits or break his seals.

This is from dust to revival — not a man nervously hanging on, but a man lifting his eyes to the God who sealed him and the Spirit who guarantees him. You are not barely making it. You are sealed for the day of redemption, kept by the Spirit of the living God, with the full inheritance certainly on its way. Lift up your eyes to the seal you bear and the Spirit you carry, and rest. You are kept. Welcome to week seven of resting in it.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust and fears it could be lost, but you are sealed for the day of redemption. Lift up your eyes — God keeps you.
carry: What would you stop worrying about if you believed God’s seal holds better than your grip?

sections.heading: The Lowest Place
pulls: You could not lift your own face off the floor. But God raised you with Christ and seated you in the heavens.
paras: Dust is the lowest place there is. It is the floor, the ground, the dirt a man’s face is pressed into when he has no strength left to rise. The psalmist’s image is exact: “My soul clings to the dust” (NKJV). And the dust is not only where a man feels low; apart from Christ, it is where he was — dead, Paul says, dead in trespasses, as low as a man can go, with no power in himself to get up. There is no self-improvement program for a corpse. A dead man cannot raise himself. If he is going to rise, Someone else must do it.

And Someone did. But God, Paul says — two of the most important words in the Bible — being rich in mercy, made his people alive together with Christ, raised them up with him, and made them to sit with him in the heavenly places. Watch the trajectory: from dead in the dust, to alive, to raised, to seated in the heavens — and all of it in Christ Jesus. The man who could not lift his own face off the floor has been carried all the way up to the throne room and given a seat. Not because he climbed, but because he was raised with Christ.

sections.heading: Already Raised, Already Seated
paras: Notice the tense again, because the dust will try to push these blessings off into the future where you cannot feel them. Paul does not say God will someday raise you and seat you if you persevere. He says God has already done it — made alive, raised up, seated — all completed, all true now, all yours in Christ. Your position is not pending. In Christ you have already been raised out of death and seated in the heavenly places, sharing even now in the life and authority of the risen Christ.

This is the plain logic of union. Because you are in Christ, his resurrection is your resurrection and his enthronement is your enthronement. Where he is, you are — positionally, really, now. The dust keeps your eyes on the floor and insists that the floor is your address. The Word lifts your eyes to the heavens and tells you that, in Christ, you are already seated there. The Christian life is the long work of learning to live on earth as a man whose true position is the throne room.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Made Alive Together With Christ
paras: Before a man can be raised, he must first be made alive, because you were dead. Paul is unsparing about the before-picture: dead in trespasses, as helpless as a corpse, contributing nothing to your own rescue. This matters because it settles forever the question of who gets the credit. A dead man does not cooperate with his own resurrection. He is acted upon. God, rich in mercy, made you alive — the same divine power that raised Jesus from the tomb reached into your spiritual grave and gave you life. You did not revive yourself. You were made alive together with Christ.

This is the deepest comfort for a man in the dust, because it means your spiritual life never depended on your strength to begin with. The God who made you alive when you were dead is not going to abandon you now that you are merely struggling. If he raised a corpse, he can certainly lift a clinging soul. The dust says you are too far gone. The Word says you were already further gone than that — you were dead — and God made you alive.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Raised With him
paras: Paul says God raised you up with him. Your union with Christ means his resurrection is not just something you admire from a distance; it is something you share. When he came out of the tomb, you came out with him. The power that raised Jesus from the dead is the same power now at work in you. Paul prays that the Ephesians would know the immeasurable greatness of God’s power toward those who believe, according to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead. That resurrection power is not reserved for a future day. It is the power already at work in the man who is in Christ.

So when the dust presses you down this week, you are not facing it with your own meager strength. You are facing it as a man raised with Christ, indwelt by the very power that emptied the tomb. The dust says you do not have the strength to rise. The Word says you have already been raised, and the strength that raised you is alive in you still.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Seated in the Heavenly Places
paras: Here is the word that lifts highest of all: God made you to sit with him in the heavenly places. Not standing at attention, not striving to climb higher — seated. A seat is the posture of arrival, of rest, of a finished work. When Christ finished his work, he sat down at the right hand of God, and in him, you are seated too. Your position in the heavenly places is not something you are straining to attain; it is something you already possess in Christ, a settled seat in the throne room while your feet still walk the dusty ground of earth.

This is why Paul tells the Colossians, since you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things above. The call is to live on earth from your true position in heaven — to stop letting the dust define your address and start living as a man whose seat is already secured at the right hand of God. You are not trying to get to the throne room. In Christ, you are already there.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to the Heights
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the floor: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). And the reviving word for a man pressed into the lowest place is raised and seated. You are not condemned to the dust. In Christ you have been made alive, raised up, and seated in the heavenly places — lifted from the floor of death to a seat at the right hand of God. Revival, for a man whose face is pressed into the dirt, begins the moment he believes he has already been raised with Christ and lifts his eyes from the floor to the seat that is already his.

So this week, when the dust presses you down and insists the floor is where you belong, lift your eyes to your true position. You have been raised with Christ. You are seated with him in the heavenly places. You are not a man trapped on the ground straining toward heaven. You are a man already seated in the heavens, learning to live on earth as one whose address is the throne room, in Christ.

stations.verse: But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved…
stations.question: Where do I still feel dead, and do I believe God made me alive together with Christ?
stations.gloss: to make alive together with
body: Syzōopoieō stacks three pieces: with, life, make. It means to make alive together with. Paul uses it only twice, both of believers made alive with Christ (Ephesians 2:5; Colossians 2:13). Look at what you were when it happened: dead through your trespasses. A dead man cannot help. He can only be raised. And he is not raised alone. He is raised with Christ.
stations.live: When your heart feels dead toward God, do not try to feel alive. Pray: “You made me alive with Christ. Stir what you made.”

stations.verse: and raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus…
stations.question: If I am seated with Christ in the heavenly places, what am I still scrambling to climb?
stations.gloss: to cause to sit down with; to sit together
body: Synkathizō means to sit down with, or to seat someone together with another. Luke uses it of people sitting down together around a fire (Luke 22:55). Paul uses it of God seating you with Christ in the heavenly places. You are not standing in line for a seat. You have been given one, beside the One who sits at the Father’s right hand. A seated man is at rest.
stations.live: Sit down before you pray this week — actually sit — and start with: “Father, I am seated with Christ.”

stations.verse: If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.
stations.question: What is my mind set on this week — the things above, or only the things on the earth?
stations.gloss: above, upward
body: Anō means above, upward. Paul uses it for the Jerusalem that is above (Galatians 4:26) and the high calling of God in Christ (Philippians 3:14). Here it gives your mind an address: seek the things that are above, where Christ is. That is not a call to ignore your work or your family. It is a call to see them from where you are seated, not from the floor.
stations.live: Three times a day this week — morning, noon, night — lift your eyes for one minute and name one thing above that is yours in Christ.

stations.verse: having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.
stations.question: Do I believe the working of God that raised Jesus is working in me now?
stations.gloss: working, operative power
body: Energeia is power at work — not strength held in reserve, but strength doing something. Paul says you were raised with Christ through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead. He says the same working works in him mightily as he labors (Colossians 1:29). Your faith is not what raises you. It rests in the God whose working does.
stations.live: Before a hard task this week, pray one sentence: “God, work in me by the working that raised Jesus.”

stations.verse: and what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to that working of the strength of his might which he worked in Christ, when he raised him from the dead and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places…
stations.question: What am I facing this week that seems bigger than the greatness of his power toward those who believe?
stations.gloss: greatness
body: Megethos means greatness, and this is its only use in the New Testament. Paul stacks words to reach it: the exceeding greatness of his power, the working of the strength of his might. Then he tells you where that power was shown — when God raised Christ from the dead and made him to sit at his right hand. That greatness is not somewhere far off. It is toward you who believe.
stations.live: Write down the biggest weight you are carrying. Beside it write Ephesians 1:19. Pray over both.

practices.title: NAME THE FLOOR YOU KEEP LIVING ON
practices.body: Most men have a low place they have accepted as their permanent address — a defeat, a discouragement, a sense that the dust is simply where they belong. This week, name yours. Where do you live face-down? Write it down, then write across it the truth from Ephesians 2: raised up with him and seated with him in the heavenly places. You cannot live from a seat you do not know you have. See it, and lift your eyes.

practices.title: SET YOUR MIND ABOVE, ON PURPOSE
practices.body: Paul commands a deliberate act: seek the things above, set your mind above. The dust pulls your gaze down by default, so the upward look must be chosen. This week, when you catch your mind fixed on the floor — on the failure, the fear, the heaviness — consciously lift it: “I have been raised with Christ. My seat is above. Set my mind there.” Practice the upward look until it becomes a habit of the soul.

practices.title: FACE THE DAY IN THE SON’S RESURRECTION POWER
practices.body: You will be tempted to face the dust with your own depleted strength and lose. Reverse it. The power that raised Christ and seated him is the same power at work in you. Pray it before the day begins: “Lord, I have been raised with you. The power that emptied your tomb is alive in me. I face this day not from weakness but from resurrection.” When the dust presses down this week, answer it: I am raised with Christ, and his power is in me.

practices.title: LET THE SPIRIT LIFT YOUR GAZE
practices.body: The Spirit who raised Jesus dwells in you and is able to lift your eyes from the dust to the throne. When you feel pressed to the floor this week, ask him: “Holy Spirit, you raised Christ and you live in me. Lift my eyes to where I am already seated. Help me live from above.” Then let him reorient your gaze upward.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER YOU ARE SEATED
practices.body: The dust convinces an isolated man that the floor is final. Before the week ends, tell a trusted brother the low place you have accepted as permanent, and ask him to remind you of your true position — raised and seated with Christ. A man pressed into the dust sometimes needs a brother to point up.

title: Raised and Seated With Him
subtitle: from dust to the heights
keyVerse: and raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus…

passage.text: You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins,
in which you once walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the children of disobedience.
We also all once lived among them in the lusts of our flesh, doing the desires of the flesh and of the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest.
But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us,
even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—
and raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,
that in the ages to come he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus;
for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God,
not of works, that no one would boast.
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first. Then answer the question honestly, and let the word study sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeIntro: This week is not about feeling lifted by Friday. It is about living from a position God already gave you. Here is how that lands in real life, with the Father, the Son, and the Spirit woven through.
lifePulls: The dust says you do not have the strength to rise. The Word says you have already been raised — and seated with Christ in the heavenly places.
prayer: Father, I spend too many days with my face on the floor. I confess I live as if the dust were my true address. Thank you that you made me alive together with Christ when I was dead. Thank you that you raised me with him and seated me with him in the heavenly places. Lift my mind to the things above today. Let me walk this ground as a man already seated. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I spend too many days with my face on the floor. I confess I live as if the dust were my true
address. Thank you that you made me alive together with Christ when I was dead. Thank you that you
raised me with him and seated me with him in the heavenly places. Lift my mind to the things above
today. Let me walk this ground as a man already seated. In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Ephesians 2:6 hands a floor-bound man the highest word in the letter: God raised you up with Christ and made you to sit with him in the heavenly places. Your feet are still on dusty ground, but your seat is already fixed. You do not climb to it. You live from it.
benediction: Brother, the dust presses your face to the floor and tells you the floor is where you belong. Lift your eyes off the ground and onto the God who raises the dead. When you were dead in trespasses, with no strength to lift even your own face, God — rich in mercy, moved by great love — made you alive together with Christ, raised you up with him, and seated you with him in the heavenly places. The man who could not rise has been carried all the way to the throne room and given a seat, not by climbing, but by being joined to the risen Christ.

So when the dust presses you down this week, lift up your eyes. When you feel too low to rise, lift up your eyes. When the floor feels like your final address, lift up your eyes to the seat that is already yours at the right hand of God. Jesus took on flesh and descended all the way to death, into the lowest place, so that he could carry you out of it. He rose, and you rose with him. He sat down at the right hand of God, and in him you are seated too. The power that emptied his tomb is the power at work in you now.

This is from dust to revival — not a man straining to climb out of the dirt, but a man lifting his eyes to a seat he has already been given in the heavens. You are not trapped on the floor. You are raised with Christ, seated with Christ, alive with his life and strong with his power, learning to live on earth as a citizen of the place where you already sit. Lift up your eyes to the throne room that is your true address, and live from the heights. Welcome to week eight of living raised.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust of the floor, but in Christ you are seated in the heavenly places. Lift up your eyes to where you already sit.
carry: What would it look like to walk into tomorrow as a man already seated with Christ?

sections.heading: The Poverty of the Dust
pulls: You are not a pauper scraping by in the dust. In Christ you are an heir of God, named in the will, with everything ahead of you.
paras: A man in the dust feels poor. Not only in his wallet, but in his soul — he feels like a man who owns nothing, who has nothing coming, who is scraping by on whatever spiritual fumes he can find and bracing for a future as empty as his present. The dust is a place of scarcity. It tells a man that there is no estate with his name on it, no inheritance coming, nothing ahead but more of the same hard ground. And so he lives small, defends his little, and never lifts his eyes to ask whether there might be something vast that is already his.

Into that poverty Paul speaks a word from the world of estates and wills: heirs. If you are a child of God, he says, then you are an heir — an heir of God and a joint heir with Christ. The man in the dust is not a pauper with nothing coming. He is an heir, named in the will of God, set to inherit not a modest allowance but everything the Father has, alongside Christ himself. The same God who adopted him as a son has written him into the inheritance, and the estate is beyond reckoning.

sections.heading: Children, Therefore Heirs
paras: Paul’s logic is simple and unbreakable: if children, then heirs. Sonship and inheritance go together. So the moment God adopted you as a son in Christ, he also made you an heir, with full legal right to the inheritance. This is not a reward you earn by good behavior; it is a status that comes automatically with being a child of God. You do not work your way up to becoming an heir. You became one the moment you became a son.

And notice the scope: heirs of God. Not merely heirs of some blessings God hands out, but heirs of God himself — heirs whose inheritance is God, his presence, his glory, his all. The dust says your future is empty. The Word says your future is God himself, and everything that is his, given to you as a joint heir with Christ. There is no poverty in that future. There is only inexhaustible wealth.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Children, Therefore Heirs
paras: The Spirit testifies, Paul says, that you are a child of God — and from that sonship the inheritance follows necessarily. This is why the dust cannot finally make you poor. Your inheritance is not based on your performance or your circumstances; it is based on your sonship, which was settled when God adopted you in Christ. A son does not lose his place in the will by having a hard week. The inheritance is tied to the relationship, and the relationship is secured in Christ. Paul says elsewhere, so you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.

This means a man can be flat broke and pressed into the dust and still be one of the wealthiest beings in the universe, because his true wealth is an inheritance kept in heaven, not a balance kept on earth. The dust measures your worth by what you have now. The Word measures it by what is coming — and what is coming, for an heir of God, is everything.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Joint Heirs With Christ
paras: Paul does not merely say you are an heir; he says you are a joint heir with Christ. This is almost too much to take in. You do not inherit a small portion off to the side while Christ inherits everything. You inherit alongside him, sharing in his inheritance, co-heirs of all that the Father has given to the Son. What belongs to Christ — the glory, the kingdom, the new creation, the inheritance of all things — is shared with those who are joined to him. Your portion is secured by his, because you inherit together with him.

This is the height of what union with Christ means for your future. Because you are in him, his inheritance becomes yours. The dust would have you believe you will always be on the outside of the wealth, your nose pressed to the glass. The Word says you are inside, a joint heir with the Son, set to inherit everything he inherits. There is no closer relationship to the estate than to be a co-heir with the One who owns it all.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: An Inheritance Kept in Heaven
paras: Peter describes the inheritance in words that answer every fear about losing it: an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you. Consider each word. Imperishable — it cannot rot or decay. Undefiled — it cannot be polluted or spoiled. Unfading — it cannot lose its beauty or value over time. And kept in heaven for you — it is not stored where moth and rust and thieves can reach it, but guarded by God himself, reserved with your name on it. This is an inheritance no economic collapse can erase, no failure can forfeit, no thief can carry off.

So when the dust threatens you with scarcity and loss, the answer is to lift your eyes to where your inheritance is kept. It is not in a place that can be ruined. It is held in heaven, guarded by God, certain and secure. The dust says you could lose everything. The Word says your true inheritance is the one thing that can never be lost, because God himself is keeping it for you.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to the Estate
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the poverty of the ground: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). And the reviving word for a man who feels he owns nothing is heir. You are not a pauper with nothing coming. In Christ you are an heir of God and a joint heir with Christ, named in the will, with an inheritance imperishable and undefiled and unfading kept in heaven for you. Revival, for a man crushed by spiritual poverty, begins the moment he lifts his eyes from his empty present to the vast estate that is already, certainly, his in Christ.

So this week, when the dust presses scarcity on your soul and tells you there is nothing ahead, lift your eyes to your inheritance. You are written into the will of God. You inherit alongside Christ. The estate is kept in heaven, guarded by God, with your name on it. You are not a poor man scraping by. You are an heir of God, and the riches that are coming cannot be measured, lost, or undone.

stations.verse: The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God; and if children, then heirs: heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him.
stations.question: If I am a joint heir with Christ, what am I clutching as if it were all I will ever have?
stations.gloss: a joint heir, a fellow inheritor
body: Synklēronomos is an heir who inherits together with another. Peter uses it for husband and wife as joint heirs of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7). Paul uses it for the most startling partnership there is: heirs of God, and joint heirs with Christ. What the Son receives, you share. Paul does not hide the road there — if indeed you suffer with him. But the road ends in being glorified with him.
stations.live: When scarcity grips you this week, say it plainly: “I am a joint heir with Christ.” Then give something away.

stations.verse: We were also assigned an inheritance in him, having been foreordained according to the purpose of him who does all things after the counsel of his will…
stations.question: Do I believe my portion in Christ was assigned on purpose, by the counsel of God’s will?
stations.gloss: to assign by lot; to give a share or portion
body: Klēroō comes from the word for a lot or allotted portion. It appears only here in the New Testament. WEB renders it: “We were also assigned an inheritance in him.” Paul ties the assignment to purpose — foreordained according to the counsel of God’s will. Your share is not luck, and it is not leftovers. It was given with intent by the One who does all things after the counsel of his will.
stations.live: Thank God this week for one part of your life you would not have chosen, and ask him to show you his purpose in it.

stations.verse: having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints…
stations.question: Do I see the hope of God’s calling, or only the weight of my own obligations?
stations.gloss: a calling; the call of God to salvation
body: Klēsis is a calling — in the New Testament, the call of God that brings a man to himself. Paul says the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29). Here he prays that the eyes of your heart would be enlightened to know the hope of his calling. The call did not start with your answer. It started with God, and what God calls, he does not take back.
stations.live: Pray Ephesians 1:18 over yourself every morning this week: “Enlighten the eyes of my heart.”

stations.verse: giving thanks to the Father, who made us fit to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light…
stations.question: Where do I still feel unqualified for the inheritance that the Father has already made me fit to share?
stations.gloss: to make sufficient, to render fit
body: Hikanoō means to make sufficient, to render fit for something. Paul uses it twice: God made him sufficient as a servant of the new covenant (2 Corinthians 3:6), and the Father made you fit to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light. The fitness is not yours. It is given. A man made fit by God does not need to prove it to anyone.
stations.live: When the old voice says you do not belong among the saints, answer with the verse: “The Father made me fit.”

stations.verse: knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.
stations.question: Whom am I really working for this week — the man over me, or the Lord Christ?
stations.gloss: a recompense, a repayment in return
body: Antapodosis is a repayment given in return, and this is its only New Testament use. Paul writes it to servants who owned nothing and inherited nothing by law. From the Lord, he tells them, you will receive the reward of the inheritance. The men with the least on earth are promised an estate. The work you do on an ordinary Tuesday is seen by the Lord you serve.
stations.live: Do one hidden job well this week — one no one will notice — and offer it to Christ by name.

practices.title: NAME THE SCARCITY YOU LIVE IN
practices.body: Most men carry a specific spiritual scarcity — “I have nothing to offer,” “there’s nothing good ahead for me,” “I’m spiritually broke.” This week, name yours. Write it down, then write across it the truth from Romans 8: heir of God and joint heir with Christ. You cannot live like an heir while you believe you are a pauper. Name the scarcity, and answer it with the will of God.

practices.title: LIVE LIKE AN HEIR, NOT A HIRED HAND
practices.body: An heir and a hired hand work very differently. The hired hand is anxious, always proving himself, afraid of being let go. The heir is secure, working from belonging rather than for it. This week, when you catch yourself living like a hired hand — striving to earn your keep with God — stop and preach your status: “I am no longer a bondservant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ.” Then work and serve from that security, not for it.

practices.title: RECEIVE THE INHERITANCE FROM THE SON
practices.body: You will be tempted to try to qualify yourself for God’s blessing. Reverse it. The Father has already qualified you to share in the inheritance, and you inherit as a joint heir with Christ. Pray it back: “Lord, I inherit with you, not by my merit but by my union with you. I receive the estate as a son.” When the scarcity lie returns this week, answer it: I am a joint heir with Christ, and the inheritance is secure.

practices.title: LET THE SPIRIT OPEN YOUR EYES TO THE RICHES
practices.body: Paul prays that the eyes of your heart would be enlightened to know the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints. This week, ask the Spirit to do exactly that: “Holy Spirit, open the eyes of my heart. Let me see the inheritance that is already mine, kept in heaven, imperishable and unfading. Lift me out of scarcity into the wealth I already have in Christ.” Then look for the riches he shows you.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER WHAT IS COMING
practices.body: Scarcity-thinking thrives in isolation. Before the week ends, tell a trusted brother the spiritual poverty you have been believing, and ask him to remind you of the inheritance that is coming. A man living small sometimes needs a brother to point to the estate.

title: Heirs of an Inheritance
subtitle: from dust to the estate
keyVerse: The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God; and if children, then heirs: heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him.

passage.text: For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.
For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!”
The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God;
and if children, then heirs: heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him.
For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first. Then answer the question honestly, and let the word study sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeIntro: This week is not about feeling rich by Friday. It is about living from an inheritance already secured. Here is how that lands in real life, with the Father, the Son, and the Spirit woven through.
lifePulls: The dust measures your worth by what you have now. The Word measures it by what is coming — and what is coming is the estate of God.
prayer: Father, I live like a hired hand counting his wages. I confess I measure my worth by what I have in my hands today. Thank you that I am your child, and if a child, then an heir. Thank you that the Father made me fit to share the inheritance of the saints in light. Open the eyes of my heart to the riches that are already mine. Let me work today for the Lord Christ. In Jesus’ name, amen.
