me fit to share the inheritance of the saints in light. Open the eyes of my heart to the riches that are
already mine. Let me work today for the Lord Christ. In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: If you are a child of God, you are an heir — an heir of God and a joint heir with Christ. The dust measures you by what is in your hands today. God measures you by an inheritance that is already assigned to you in him.
benediction: Brother, the dust is a place of poverty, and it works hard to convince you that you own nothing and have nothing coming — that your future is as empty as the hard ground your soul clings to. Lift your eyes off that scarcity and onto the estate of God. The moment the Father adopted you as a son in Christ, he wrote you into his will, making you an heir of God and a joint heir with Christ. You do not inherit a modest portion off to the side; you inherit alongside the Son, sharing in everything the Father has given him. The estate is beyond reckoning, and your name is on it.

So when the dust presses scarcity on your soul this week, lift up your eyes. When you feel spiritually broke with nothing ahead, lift up your eyes. When the future looks empty, lift up your eyes to an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, unfading, and kept in heaven for you. Jesus, the heir of all things, took on flesh and became poor — so poor he had nowhere to lay his head, so poor he was stripped even of his garments on the cross — so that you, through his poverty, might become rich. He shared your poverty so that you could share his inheritance.

This is from dust to revival — not a man scraping together what little he can find, but a man lifting his eyes to the vast estate already his as a joint heir with Christ. You are not poor. You are an heir of God, named in the will, with riches imperishable and certain ahead of you. Lift up your eyes to the inheritance kept for you in heaven, and live as the wealthy man you already are in Christ. Welcome to week nine of living like an heir.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust and feels poor, but in Christ you are an heir of God. Lift up your eyes to the inheritance kept for you.
carry: What are you clutching today because you forgot you are an heir of God?

pulls: Your security was never your grip on God. It was always his grip on you. And his grip does not slip.
paras: There is a particular dust a man tastes at two in the morning, when the house is quiet and his defenses are down. It is the fear of being dropped. He has heard that he is saved, that he belongs to God, that he is an heir — but a thin, cold voice keeps asking the same question: for how long? What if I drift too far? What if I sin one time too many? What if God finally has enough of me and lets go? The man lies there doing the math on his own faithfulness, and the math never comes out clean. His soul clings to the dust because he is secretly certain that one day his grip on God will fail, and on that day he will be lost.
Here is what Scripture says to that man. Your security was never your grip on God. It was always his grip on you. And his grip does not slip.

Hear Paul at the end of Romans 8, after eight chapters of building the case for everyone God justifies: “For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39). Read that list again slowly. It is a lantern carried through every room of the universe, looking for one thing that could separate you from God — and finding the rooms empty. Death searched: cannot. Life searched: cannot. Angels, rulers, powers, the present, the future, the heights, the depths, every created thing searched: cannot, cannot, cannot. Paul turns over every created thing and finds nothing with the strength to pry you out of the love of God in Christ.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Fear Underneath the Dust
paras: Most men will not say it out loud, but they live as though their salvation hangs by a thread they themselves are holding. They imagine a great chain of grace lowered down from heaven, and at the very bottom link, the place where the chain meets the man, there is a clasp that only the man can keep shut. So he white-knuckles his own salvation. He measures his standing with God by the quality of his last week. A good week, and he feels held. A bad week, and he feels the clasp loosening.

This is exhausting, and it is also a lie. It makes a man the weakest link in his own redemption, and a chain held by a frightened, sinful man would have snapped the first afternoon. But the gospel does not hang your salvation on your grip. Jesus said of his sheep, “I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father who has given them to me is greater than all. No one is able to snatch them out of my Father’s hand” (John 10:28–29). Notice whose hands are doing the holding. The Son’s hand and the Father’s hand — a double grip of omnipotence around one trembling sheep. The sheep is not asked to hold on. The sheep is held.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Nothing in the List
paras: Look hard at Paul’s list in Romans 8, because he built it on purpose to cover every fear a man has ever had at two in the morning. Death — the thing that ends every other earthly security — cannot separate you. Life — with all its long, grinding seasons, its slow backslides, its disappointing years — cannot separate you. Angels and principalities and powers — every spiritual power, every accusation of the accuser — cannot separate you. Things present — your sin today, your failure this very afternoon — cannot. Things to come — the sin you have not yet committed, the collapse you secretly fear is coming — cannot. Height and depth — whether you are riding high or scraping the bottom — cannot. And then Paul, as if to leave no crack unsealed, adds “nor any other created thing.” If it is created, it is on the list. And if it is on the list, it cannot separate you from the love of God in Christ.

Read your own name into the empty space. Whatever you were about to offer as the exception — “but what about my...” — is a created thing, and Paul already searched it and found it powerless. There is no asterisk. There is no fine print. There is no clause that begins “unless.”

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Who Does the Keeping
paras: If you are kept, the next question is everything: kept by whom? Because if the keeping is finally up to you, then you are not kept at all; you are only on probation. But Scripture lays the keeping squarely on God. Peter writes that you are among those “who by the power of God are guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time” (1 Peter 1:5). Guarded by God’s power — not your willpower, not your performance, not your perfect record, but the power of God himself standing watch over your soul. Paul says it again to the Philippians: “he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). The One who started your salvation has taken personal responsibility to finish it. He does not begin what he will not complete. He does not save halfway and dare you to keep the rest.

This is why the doctrine men sometimes call “eternal security” is not a license to coast; it is a foundation to build on. A son who knows his father will never disown him does not love his father less — he serves from rest instead of fear. The grip of God is not a hammock for the lazy. It is bedrock for the weary.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to the Grip of God
paras: So here is the turn, the same turn this whole study keeps making. Psalm 119:25 says, “My soul clings to the dust” (NKJV). Picture that clinging hand — desperate, white-knuckled, terrified of slipping. That is the man who thinks his security depends on how tightly he can hold on. Now look up from your own clinging hand to the hands of God closed around you — the Son’s hand and the Father’s hand, a double grip of omnipotence that no created thing can break. Your clinging was never what kept you. His grip was. And his grip does not slip, does not tire, does not loosen at two in the morning when your faith feels thin.

That is from dust to the grip of God. Not a man holding on for dear life, but a man held by the One who is life. “Revive me according to Your word,” the psalmist prays — and the word revives by telling the clinging man the truth: you are not holding God; God is holding you, and he will not let go.

stations.verse: For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
stations.question: What is the one thing I keep adding to Paul’s list as the exception that could separate me from God’s love?
stations.gloss: height; that which is lifted up
body: Hypsōma means height, something lifted up. Paul uses it once for every high thing raised against the knowledge of God (2 Corinthians 10:5). In Romans 8 it sits in the list: nor height, nor depth. Nothing up high and nothing down low — no power above you and no pit beneath you — can separate you from God’s love in Christ Jesus. Then Paul closes the list: nor any other created thing.
stations.live: Name your own exception out loud. Then read Romans 8:38–39 over it, slowly, and put it on the list.

stations.verse: I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father who has given them to me is greater than all. No one is able to snatch them out of my Father’s hand.
stations.question: If no one can snatch me out of the Father’s hand, what am I afraid will carry me off?
stations.gloss: to seize, snatch away, carry off by force
body: Harpazō means to seize and carry off by force. Jesus uses it a few verses earlier for the wolf that snatches the sheep (John 10:12). Then he uses it again with a promise: no one will snatch them out of my hand. No one is able to snatch them out of my Father’s hand. The wolf is real. The hand is stronger. Two hands hold you — the Son’s and the Father’s.
stations.live: Name the thing you fear will carry you off. Then say: “It cannot snatch me out of my Father’s hand.”

stations.verse: This is the will of my Father who sent me, that of all he has given to me I should lose nothing, but should raise him up at the last day.
stations.question: Do I believe it is the Father’s will that Christ should lose nothing of all the Father gave him?
stations.gloss: to destroy; to lose utterly; to be lost
body: Apollymi means to lose, or to be lost. Jesus uses it for the sheep the shepherd goes after until he finds it (Luke 15:4). Here he states his Father’s will: of all he has given to me I should lose nothing. At his arrest John records it done: of those you have given me, I have lost none (John 18:9). Your keeping rests on the will of the Father and the faithfulness of the Son.
stations.live: Before you sleep this week, pray John 6:39 back to Jesus: “You will lose nothing the Father gave you. I am his gift to you.”

stations.verse: For this cause I also suffer these things. Yet I am not ashamed, for I know him whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to guard that which I have committed to him against that day.
stations.question: Have I actually committed my soul to Christ, or am I still trying to guard it myself?
stations.gloss: a deposit, something entrusted to another
body: Parathēkē is a deposit — something handed to another for safekeeping. Paul uses it for the gospel entrusted to Timothy (1 Timothy 6:20). Here he uses it of himself, in prison, facing death: I am persuaded that he is able to guard that which I have committed to him against that day. Paul’s confidence is not in his grip. It is in the One holding the deposit.
stations.live: Pray it in so many words this week: “Lord, I commit my soul to you. Guard it until that day.”

stations.verse: Now to him who is able to keep them from stumbling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory in great joy, to God our Savior, who alone is wise, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and forever. Amen.
stations.question: When I picture standing before God, do I picture stumbling in, or being presented faultless?
stations.gloss: not stumbling, sure-footed
body: Aptaistos means not stumbling — sure-footed. It appears only here. Jude closes a letter full of warnings with praise to him who is able to keep you from stumbling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory in great joy. The keeping belongs to God, and so does the presenting. The joy at the end is his joy, over what he kept.
stations.live: Memorize Jude 24–25 this week. Say it last thing at night.

practices.title: STOP DOING THE MATH ON YOUR OWN FAITHFULNESS
practices.body: Many men keep a running ledger of their spiritual performance and read their security off the bottom line. This week, close that ledger. When you catch yourself calculating whether you have been good enough to still be saved, stop and say: “My security is not my grip on God; it is his grip on me.” You were never the one holding the chain shut. Quit checking the clasp you do not control, and rest in the hands you cannot pry open.

practices.title: PREACH THE LIST TO YOURSELF
practices.body: Memorize Romans 8:38-39 this week — actually memorize it, word for word. Then, when the two-in-the-morning fear comes, preach the list out loud against your own dread. Death? Cannot. Life? Cannot. Things to come? Cannot. The thing you fear most? It is a created thing, and it is on the list, and it cannot. Let the Father, who searched all creation for an exception and found none, settle your soul.

practices.title: RECEIVE THE DOUBLE GRIP FROM THE SON
practices.body: The Son holds you, and the Father holds you, and no one can snatch you from either hand. This week, when you feel yourself slipping, pray it back to Jesus: “Lord, I am not holding you; you are holding me. The Son’s hand and the Father’s hand are closed around me, and no power can force them open. I rest in your grip, not mine.” Then go to sleep in the hands of God.

practices.title: LET THE SPIRIT TURN SECURITY INTO OBEDIENCE
practices.body: The grip of God is not a reason to coast; it is a reason to run. A man who knows he cannot be dropped is freed to obey out of love instead of fear. This week, ask the Spirit to make your security a springboard: “Holy Spirit, because I am kept and cannot be lost, free me to obey from rest. Let me serve my Father as a secure son, not a frightened hireling.” Then watch how obedience flows easier from a man who is sure of his Father.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER WHAT IS HOLDING HIM
practices.body: Some brother near you is lying awake doing the math, certain his grip is failing. Before the week ends, tell him the truth: it was never your grip, brother; it is his, and his does not slip. Point him to the hands of God closed around him. A man drowning in the fear of being dropped sometimes needs another man to show him the hands that are holding him.

title: Kept and Cannot Be Lost
subtitle: from dust to the grip of God
keyVerse: For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

passage.text: What then shall we say about these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?
He who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things?
Who could bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? It is God who justifies.
Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, yes rather, who was raised from the dead, who is at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us.
Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?
Even as it is written, “For your sake we are killed all day long. We were accounted as sheep for the slaughter.”
No, in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers,
nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first. Then answer the question honestly, and let the word study sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeIntro: The truth that you cannot be lost is meant to change how a man lives, prays, and sleeps. Here is how to walk it out this week.
lifePulls: The sheep is not asked to hold on. The sheep is held.
prayer: Father, I do the math on my own faithfulness, and it never comes out clean. I confess I have trusted my grip instead of your hand. Thank you that nothing in all creation can separate me from your love in Christ. Thank you that no one can snatch me out of your hand, and that your Son will lose none you gave him. Guard what I have committed to you. Keep me from stumbling. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I do the math on my own faithfulness, and it never comes out clean. I confess I have trusted my
grip instead of your hand. Thank you that nothing in all creation can separate me from your love in
Christ. Thank you that no one can snatch me out of your hand, and that your Son will lose none you gave
him. Guard what I have committed to you. Keep me from stumbling. In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Romans 8:38–39 carries a lantern through the whole universe looking for one thing strong enough to separate you from God’s love in Christ, and it finds nothing. Your security was never your grip on God. It is his grip on you, and no one can snatch you out of the Father’s hand.
benediction: Brother, the dust whispers its cruelest lie in the dark: that you are holding on by a thread, and one day the thread will break, and you will be lost. Lift your eyes off that thread and onto the hands of God. Jesus did not come to give you a salvation you must keep by your own strength. He came to take you into his hand and to put you, with him, into the Father’s hand — a double grip of omnipotence around one fragile sheep. He says you will never perish, and that no one is able to snatch you out. Not death, not life, not the accuser, not your worst sin, not your darkest two-in-the-morning fear. Nothing in all creation has the strength to pry open the hand of God.

So when the dust tells you that you are slipping, lift up your eyes. When you lie awake doing the math on your own faithfulness, lift up your eyes. When the fear of being dropped comes for your soul, lift up your eyes to the One who took on flesh, who let cruel hands drive nails through his own hands so that his grip on you would be purchased in blood, who rose with those nail-scarred hands to hold you forever. The hands that hold you are the hands that were pierced for you. They do not let go.

This is from dust to the grip of God — not a man clinging by his fingernails, terrified of falling, but a man held fast by hands that were wounded to keep him. You cannot be lost, because the One holding you cannot be overpowered, and he will not let go. If you miss this, you miss everything: your security is not in how well you hold him, but in how well he holds you — and he holds you with pierced and almighty hands. Lift up your eyes to the grip of God, and rest. Welcome to week ten of living as a man who cannot be lost.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust as if your grip were all that held you. Lift up your eyes — his hands hold you, and they were pierced to do it.
carry: What would you let go of if you believed no one can snatch you out of the Father’s hand?

pulls: You are not missing a piece. In Christ, you are already full.
paras: There is a dust that does not feel like sin so much as lack. A man can be doing everything right and still wake up with the gnawing sense that he is not enough — not spiritual enough, not mature enough, not far enough along, not complete. He looks at other men and feels behind. He looks at his own walk and feels like a half-finished house, framed but never finished, always one more thing away from being whole. So he goes looking for the missing piece. A new discipline, a deeper experience, a secret the other men seem to have. He is sure that somewhere out there is the part of him that is still missing, and if he could just find it, he would finally be complete.
To that man, Colossians says something almost too good to take in. You are not missing a piece. In Christ, you are already full.

Hear Paul: “For in him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily, and in him you are made full, who is the head of all principality and power” (Colossians 2:9–10). Sit with the logic of those two verses. First, the whole fullness of God dwells in Christ — not a portion, not an emanation, but the entire fullness of deity, in bodily form, in Jesus. There is no more of God to be had than is found in Christ. And then the hinge: “in him you are made full.” The same fullness that dwells in Christ is the fullness you have been brought into. You are not standing outside the storehouse with your nose against the glass. You are inside, in Christ, filled with the fullness that fills him.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Lie of the Missing Piece
paras: The dust of incompleteness is one of the most religious lies a man can believe, because it dresses up as humility and drives him to work. He thinks he is being faithful by always striving for more, never satisfied, always reaching. But underneath the striving is a quiet unbelief: a refusal to accept that Christ has already made him full. The false teachers at Colossae ran the same play. They told the church that faith in Christ was a fine start, but to be truly complete you needed something extra — special knowledge, rule-keeping, the worship of angels, a higher tier of spirituality. Paul’s whole letter is a hammer against that lie. He says the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are all hidden in Christ (Colossians 2:3), so why go looking elsewhere? He says you are made full in Christ, so why live like you are empty?

The missing-piece lie always points you away from Christ to find your completeness. The gospel always points you back into Christ, where the completeness already is. Every voice that says “Christ plus this” is selling you something you already own.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Filled With the Fullness
paras: What does it mean that “in him you are made full”? It does not mean you have arrived at sinless perfection or that there is no more growing to do. It means your standing before God is complete — that in Christ you lack nothing required to belong to God, to be loved by him, to be his. Paul prays elsewhere that the Ephesians would be “filled with all the fullness of God” (Ephesians 3:19), and John says of Christ, “From his fullness we all received grace upon grace” (John 1:16). The picture is not a man begging at the door for scraps of God. It is a man brought inside the inexhaustible fullness of Christ and told: it is all yours, draw from it, grace upon grace, and it never runs dry.

A man who believes this stops striving to become complete and starts living from a completeness he already has. He does not chase the missing piece, because there is no missing piece. He grows, not to become full, but because he is full — the way a tree that is alive puts out leaves, not to earn its life, but because it has it.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Complete Means Christ Is Enough
paras: Here is the sharp edge of “complete in him.” If you are complete in Christ, then Christ is enough. Not Christ plus your performance. Not Christ plus a peak experience. Not Christ plus the approval of other men. Just Christ. The reason men feel perpetually incomplete is that they have quietly added requirements to their wholeness that God never added. They have decided they will be complete when they finally beat the sin, when they finally feel close to God, when they finally measure up to the man across the room. But God says you are complete now, in Christ, who is the head of all rule and authority. The head of all principality and power has made you full, and no lesser authority gets to declare you empty.

This is why “complete in him” is such firm ground for a man still wrestling with sin. You can put your sin to death with your whole strength precisely because your completeness does not hang on how today goes. You are not working to become whole. You are working as a whole man in Christ who refuses to live like a fragment.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to Fullness
paras: Now the turn. “My soul clings to the dust,” says Psalm 119:25 (NKJV) — and few forms of dust cling harder than the sense of never being enough, the half-finished feeling that drives a man to chase completeness everywhere but where it actually is. Lift your eyes off the missing piece you keep hunting and onto the fullness that already fills you in Christ. The whole fullness of deity dwells in him, and you are made full in him. You were a half-built house clinging to the dust; in Christ you are filled with the fullness of God, complete, lacking nothing for belonging to your Father.

That is from dust to fullness — not a man forever hunting the piece that will finally make him whole, but a man who has discovered that in Christ he was made whole already. “Revive me according to Your word,” prays the psalmist — and the word revives by telling the half-finished man the truth: you are complete in him. Stop hunting. Start drawing from the fullness that is already yours.

stations.verse: For in him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily, and in him you are made full, who is the head of all principality and power.
stations.question: What am I adding to Christ, as if the fullness of the Deity dwelling in him were not enough?
stations.gloss: deity, the nature of God
body: Theotēs means deity — what God is. It appears only here in the New Testament. Paul does not say something of God dwells in Christ. He says all the fullness of the Deity dwells in him bodily. Then comes the turn: in him you are made full. There is nothing left over outside Christ that you need to go find. Everything God is dwells in the One you are in.
stations.live: When you feel you need Christ plus something, name the plus. Then say: “In him I am made full.”

stations.verse: and to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
stations.question: Do I treat Christ’s love as something I have already measured?
stations.gloss: to exceed, surpass, go beyond
body: Hyperballō means to throw beyond — to exceed, to surpass. Paul uses it for the exceeding riches of God’s grace (Ephesians 2:7) and here for Christ’s love, which surpasses knowledge. He prays that you would know a love you cannot finish knowing. You will not come to the end of it. The man who thinks he has measured Christ’s love has not yet seen it.
stations.live: Each day this week, name one way Christ’s love reached you that you did not see coming.

stations.verse: From his fullness we all received grace upon grace.
stations.question: Where am I living as though grace ran out yesterday?
stations.gloss: in place of, instead of, for
body: Anti means in place of, one thing for another. It is the word in Mark 10:45: the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many. In John 1:16 it describes grace: grace upon grace — one grace given in place of the last, and another after that. From his fullness you received, and you keep receiving. The supply does not run down.
stations.live: When you feel spiritually empty this week, pray John 1:16: “From your fullness, give me grace upon grace today.”

stations.verse: in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.
stations.question: Where am I hunting for wisdom everywhere except in Christ?
stations.gloss: hidden, stored away
body: Apokryphos means hidden, stored away. Jesus says there is nothing hidden that will not be made known (Mark 4:22). Paul says all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ. Not scattered. Not locked away from ordinary men. Stored in a Person, and opened to those who are in him. You do not need a secret teaching. You need Christ, and more of him.
stations.live: Bring your hardest decision this week to Christ in prayer before you bring it to anyone else.

stations.verse: seeing that his divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and virtue…
stations.question: What do I think I still lack for life and godliness that God has not already granted?
stations.gloss: to give, to bestow as a gift
body: Dōreomai means to give as a gift. Mark uses it when Pilate granted Jesus’ body to Joseph (Mark 15:45). Peter uses it twice in two verses: his divine power has granted to you all things that pertain to life and godliness, and he has granted his precious and exceedingly great promises. All things. Given. Not loaned against your performance.
stations.live: Make a short list of what you think you are missing. Beside each, write 2 Peter 1:3, and ask God to show you what he has already given.

practices.title: NAME THE “MISSING PIECE” YOU KEEP CHASING
practices.body: Most men have a specific thing they believe will finally make them complete — beat this sin, reach this milestone, feel this closeness, match this other man. This week, name yours out loud. Then write over it the truth of Colossians 2:10: you are made full in him. Whatever you named is not the missing piece to your completeness; in Christ you are already complete, and the hunting can stop.

practices.title: STOP LIVING “CHRIST PLUS” AND LIVE “CHRIST ALONE”
practices.body: Every form of incompleteness sneaks in an addition: Christ plus performance, Christ plus experience, Christ plus approval. This week, catch the addition. When you feel that you need something more than Christ to be whole, name it and renounce it: “I am complete in Christ alone. I do not need Christ plus anything to be full.” Then rest in the sufficiency of the One in whom all fullness dwells.

practices.title: DRAW FROM THE FULLNESS IN THE SON
practices.body: You are not standing outside the storehouse; you are inside it, in Christ. This week, practice drawing from his fullness instead of striving in your emptiness. When you feel spiritually empty, pray it back: “Lord, from your fullness I receive grace upon grace. I draw from you, not from my own dry well. Fill me from the fullness that is already mine in you.” Then receive, wave after wave.

practices.title: LET THE SPIRIT MAKE YOU FULL, NOT FRANTIC
practices.body: Restless striving for completeness is a kind of unbelief; the Spirit replaces it with rest. This week, ask him: “Holy Spirit, fill me with all the fullness of God. Quiet the frantic hunt for more, and let me live from the completeness Christ has already given me.” Then notice how the striving loosens when you believe you are already full.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER HE IS ALREADY COMPLETE
practices.body: Some brother near you is exhausted from chasing the missing piece, sure he is not enough. Before the week ends, remind him: brother, in Christ you are already complete; you are not missing a thing required to belong to God. Point him off the hunt and back into the fullness. A man worn out from striving to be whole sometimes needs another man to tell him he already is.

title: Complete in Him
subtitle: from dust to fullness
keyVerse: For in him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily, and in him you are made full, who is the head of all principality and power.

passage.text: As therefore you received Christ Jesus, the Lord, walk in him,
rooted and built up in him, and established in the faith, even as you were taught, abounding in it in thanksgiving.
Be careful that you don’t let anyone rob you through his philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the elements of the world, and not after Christ.
For in him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily,
and in him you are made full, who is the head of all principality and power.
In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, in the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ,
having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.
You were dead through your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh. He made you alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses,
wiping out the handwriting in ordinances which was against us. He has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.
Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first. Then answer the question honestly, and let the word study sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeIntro: The truth that you are complete in Christ is meant to end a man’s restless hunting and ground him in fullness. Here is how to walk it out.
lifePulls: Every voice that says ‘Christ plus this’ is selling you something you already own.
prayer: Father, I keep hunting for the missing piece, as if Christ were not enough. I confess I have chased fullness in places that only left me emptier. Thank you that all the fullness of the Deity dwells in Christ, and that in him I am made full. Thank you for grace upon grace. Quiet my restless searching today. Let me live from what you have already given. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I keep hunting for the missing piece, as if Christ were not enough. I confess I have chased
fullness in places that only left me emptier. Thank you that all the fullness of the Deity dwells in Christ,
and that in him I am made full. Thank you for grace upon grace. Quiet my restless searching today. Let
me live from what you have already given. In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: In Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily, and in him you are made full. You are not missing a piece. Every voice that says “Christ plus this” is selling you what you already own.
benediction: Brother, the dust has a way of convincing a good man that he is a fragment — framed but unfinished, always one piece short of whole — and so he spends his strength hunting for the part of himself that is missing. Lift your eyes off that endless hunt and onto the fullness of Christ. In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily; there is no more of God to be found anywhere than is found in Jesus. And the gospel’s unthinkable word to you is that you are made full in him. You are not outside the fullness pressing your face to the glass. You are inside it, in Christ, filled with the fullness that fills him.

So when the dust tells you that you are not enough, lift up your eyes. When you feel like a half-built house, lift up your eyes. When you are tempted to go hunting for the missing piece in some experience or discipline or another man’s approval, lift up your eyes to the One in whom all the treasures are hidden and all the fullness dwells. The fullness of God did not stay at an unreachable height. It came down, it took on flesh, it dwelt bodily in Jesus, it went to the cross to bring empty men into its fullness — and it drew you inside. You are complete because he is complete, and you are in him.

This is from dust to fullness — not a man forever short of whole, scrambling after the piece that will finally complete him, but a man who has discovered that in Christ he was made full already. If you miss this, you miss everything: your completeness is not Christ plus something else, but Christ alone, in whom the whole fullness of God was pleased to dwell. Lift up your eyes to that fullness, stop hunting, and draw from the One who has filled you. Welcome to week eleven of living as a complete man in Christ.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust and feels like it is never enough. Lift up your eyes — in Christ the whole fullness of God dwells, and in him you are made full.
carry: What have you been adding to Christ that he never asked you to carry?

pulls: For eleven weeks the word was that you are in Christ. Now comes the reverse: Christ is in you.
paras: You come now to the last week of this study, and there is a particular dust that belongs to the end of a long road. It is the weariness of a man who has walked a great distance and is not yet home. Eleven weeks ago you began in the dust of Psalm 119:25, a soul flat on the ground, and week by week you have lifted your eyes — to union, to belonging, to ransom, to acquittal, to new birth, to the table, to security, to the heights, to the inheritance, to the unbreakable grip of God, to fullness. And still, if a man is honest, there is a stretch of road left. He is not yet glorified. He still sins, still struggles, still feels the dust under him on the hard days. He believes the riches are real, but the final glory still feels far off, like a city whose lights he can see but whose gates he has not reached.

To that weary man on the long road, Colossians speaks the final word of this whole study — and it is the most intimate word of all. God was pleased “to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Colossians 1:27). For eleven weeks the word has been that you are in Christ. Now, at the end, comes the reverse: Christ is in you. And because he is in you, glory is not a distant maybe. It is a settled hope — not wishful thinking, but a guaranteed future — carried inside you by the Person of Christ himself.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Mystery Finally Spoken
paras: Paul calls it a mystery — something hidden for ages and now revealed. The mystery is not a riddle to be solved but a Person to be received, and the revelation is shockingly personal: Christ in you. Not Christ far off in heaven, not Christ merely as a historical figure, not Christ as an idea you admire — but Christ himself, by his Spirit, taking up residence in the life of an ordinary man still clinging to the dust on his hard days. The riches of the glory of this mystery come down to four words: Christ in you. Everything this study has unfolded — every benefit, every blessing, every chapter of the wealth that is yours in Christ — is finally secured by this: the Christ who holds all those riches lives in you.

This is why Paul calls it “the riches of the glory.” It is not a modest indwelling. It is the whole weight of Christ’s glory, taking up residence in a clay jar. You have this treasure in clay vessels, Paul says elsewhere, so that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God and not from you. The dust does not disqualify you from the indwelling. The dust is exactly the kind of jar God delights to fill with his glory.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The Hope That Cannot Disappoint
paras: “Christ in you, the hope of glory.” Notice that Christ himself is the hope. Your hope of finally reaching glory is not your own perseverance, not your slow improvement, not your odds of staying faithful to the end. Your hope of glory is a Person living inside you, and he does not fail. Biblical hope is not crossed fingers; it is settled certainty about a future God has guaranteed. And the guarantee is bolted to the indwelling Christ: because he is in you now, glory is where you are surely headed. “When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory” (Colossians 3:4). He is your life now; therefore you will appear with him in glory then. The indwelling now secures the glory then.

This is the answer to the weariness of the long road. The man is right that he is not yet glorified — but he is wrong to think the outcome is in doubt. The One who guarantees the destination is not waiting at the end of the road; he is walking it from the inside. Christ in you is the down payment and the guarantee of Christ revealed in glory. The lights of the city are not a distant maybe. The King of the city lives in you, and he is bringing you home.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Becoming What You Will Behold
paras: What is this glory you are headed toward? Scripture says it is nothing less than being made like Christ. “Beloved, now we are children of God. It is not yet revealed what we will be; but we know that when he is revealed, we will be like him; for we will see him just as he is” (1 John 3:2). The glory is to see him as he is and, in seeing him, to be made fully like him at last — every remnant of dust burned away, the image of Christ complete in you. And the process has already begun. “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Even now, the indwelling Christ is changing you, degree by degree, into his likeness. The glory ahead is not a sudden stranger; it is the finished form of what the Spirit is already working in you today.

So the man on the long road is not standing still. Every time he beholds Christ, he is being changed into Christ’s image, one degree at a time. The transformation is slow because it is real, but it is sure because the One doing it lives inside him and does not quit.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to Glory
paras: Here is the final turn of the whole study. “My soul clings to the dust,” Psalm 119:25 began (NKJV) — a man face down on the hard ground, unable to rise. For twelve weeks you have lifted your eyes off that dust and onto the riches that are yours in Christ. And now the road runs all the way to its end: from dust to glory. The man who started flat on the ground, clinging to the dust, is headed for the unveiled presence of Christ, to be made like him, to appear with him in glory. And the guarantee that he will arrive is not his own strength but the Christ who lives in him. Christ in you is the hope of glory — the certainty that the road from dust ends not in more dust but in glory, because the One carrying you is glory himself.

“Revive me according to Your word,” the psalmist prayed twelve weeks ago, and the whole study has been God’s answer. He revives the dust-clinging man by union with his Son, and he will finish the reviving in glory, when the Christ who lives in him now is revealed, and the man appears with him, made like him at last. That is the arc: from dust to glory. It is the road you are on. And the One who is your hope of reaching the end is already home inside you.

stations.verse: to whom God was pleased to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
stations.question: Do I live as though Christ is actually in me, or only somewhere above me?
stations.gloss: a mystery; a truth once hidden, now revealed by God
body: Mystērion in Paul does not mean a puzzle. It means a truth once hidden that God has now made known. Paul says it had been hidden for ages and generations but is now revealed to his saints (Colossians 1:26). And he names it: Christ in you, the hope of glory. The secret God kept is not a technique. It is a Person, and he lives in you.
stations.live: Say it to yourself each morning this week before anything else: “Christ in me, the hope of glory.”

stations.verse: When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory.
stations.question: If I will be revealed with Christ in glory, what am I trying to prove about myself now?
stations.gloss: to make visible, reveal, make manifest
body: Phaneroō means to make visible, to bring into the open. John uses it at Cana: Jesus revealed his glory (John 2:11). Paul uses it twice in one verse: when Christ, your life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory. Your life is hidden now. It will not stay hidden. When he is seen, you will be seen with him, as you truly are in him.
stations.live: Stop managing how you are seen this week. Do one good thing where no one will know, and leave the revealing to Christ.

stations.verse: Beloved, now we are children of God. It is not yet revealed what we will be; but we know that when he is revealed, we will be like him; for we will see him just as he is.
stations.question: Does knowing that I will be like him change how I carry my failures today?
stations.gloss: like, resembling, of the same kind
body: Homoios means like, resembling. Jesus used it for the Kingdom: the Kingdom of Heaven is like treasure hidden in the field (Matthew 13:44). John uses it for your future: when he is revealed, you will be like him, for you will see him just as he is. The end is not you improved. The end is you made like Christ, and it comes by seeing him.
stations.live: When you fail this week, confess it plainly, then say: “I will be like him, because I will see him.”

stations.verse: But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.
stations.question: Am I spending my time looking at the glory of the Lord, or only at myself?
stations.gloss: to look as in a mirror; to reflect like a mirror
body: Katoptrizō is tied to the word for a mirror. It appears only here. The lexicon allows it to mean looking as in a mirror or reflecting like one; WEB reads: seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror. Either way the point holds. You are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, and the change comes from the Lord, the Spirit, as you look at him.
stations.live: Give the first ten minutes of each day this week to reading about Christ in the Gospels — not about yourself.

stations.verse: But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.
stations.question: Am I embarrassed by the clay, or amazed at the treasure God put in it?
stations.gloss: made of clay, earthen
body: Ostrakinos means made of clay — earthenware, the cheap pots of an ordinary house. Paul uses it for vessels of honor and dishonor in a great house (2 Timothy 2:20). Here he uses it for you: you have this treasure in clay vessels. The clay is the dust you are made of. The treasure is the light of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. The weakness of the jar shows whose power it is.
stations.live: When your weakness shows this week, do not hide it. Thank God that the power is his and not yours.

practices.title: PREACH “CHRIST IN YOU” AGAINST THE WEARINESS
practices.body: When the long road wears you down and glory feels far off, stop and preach the mystery: Christ is in me, the hope of glory. Your hope of reaching the end was never your stamina; it is the Christ who lives in you and is bringing you home. This week, every time the destination feels doubtful, answer the doubt with the indwelling Christ. The One who is your hope of glory is already inside you.

practices.title: BEHOLD HIM, AND LET THE SPIRIT CHANGE YOU
practices.body: You are transformed into Christ’s image by beholding his glory, not by gritting your teeth. This week, give real time to beholding him — in the Word, in prayer, in worship — and trust the Spirit to do the slow metamorphosis. Pray it back: “Lord, I behold your glory; change me into your image, from glory to glory. I cannot transform myself, but the Spirit in me can, and will.” Then stop straining and start beholding.

practices.title: LIVE TODAY FROM A GUARANTEED TOMORROW
practices.body: God speaks of your glorification as already done. This week, let that settled future change your present. When you fail, remember you are still headed for glory. When you suffer, remember it is preparing for you an eternal weight of glory. Live as a man whose arrival is guaranteed, not a man still auditioning for heaven. The glorified ending is sure, because the God who justified you has already, in his reckoning, glorified you.

practices.title: LET THE FATHER, SON, AND SPIRIT CARRY YOU HOME
practices.body: The whole study has walked you through the work of the three Persons — the Father who chose and adopted you, the Son in whom you have every benefit, the Spirit who seals and transforms you. This week, rest in the truth that all three are committed to bringing you to glory. The Father predestined it, the Son indwells you as the hope of it, the Spirit is working it out degree by degree. You are not carrying yourself home. The Triune God is carrying you.

practices.title: HAND THE RICHES TO ANOTHER MAN
practices.body: You have spent twelve weeks discovering the riches that are yours in Christ. Do not bury them. Before this study ends, sit down with one man who is still clinging to the dust and hand him what you have been given. Tell him he is in Christ, that Christ is in him, that his road runs from dust to glory. The riches multiply when they are shared. A man who has been lifted out of the dust is meant to reach back and lift another.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first. Then answer the question honestly, and let the word study sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeIntro: This is the last week, so let the application reach past these seven days and into the rest of the road. Here is how to walk from dust to glory.
lifePulls: The lights of the city are not a distant maybe. The King of the city lives in you, and he is bringing you home.
prayer: Father, I am a clay jar, and the dust still shows. I confess I grow tired on the long road and forget where it ends. Thank you for the mystery you have made known: Christ in me, the hope of glory. Thank you that when he is revealed, I will be revealed with him and made like him. Keep my eyes on his glory until you change me into his image. Revive me according to your word, all the way home. In Jesus’ name, amen.

bottomLine: Christ in you is the hope of glory. For twelve weeks the word has been that you are in him; now it is that he is in you, and he is the guarantee of where the road ends. When he is revealed, you will be revealed with him and made like him.
benediction: Brother, you began twelve weeks ago with a soul face down in the dust, praying the prayer of Psalm 119:25: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). And week by week, the word has done exactly what it promised — it has revived you, not by improving the dust, but by joining you to the One who is life. You have lifted your eyes to union, to belonging, to ransom, to no condemnation, to new birth, to the table of reconciliation, to the seal of the Spirit, to the heights where you are seated with him, to an inheritance kept in heaven, to a grip that cannot be broken, to a fullness that lacks nothing. And now, at the end, you lift your eyes to the most intimate riches of all: Christ in you, the hope of glory.

This was always where the road was going. Every benefit in this study — every blessing, every riches of the wealth that is yours in Christ — has been pointing here, to the Person who holds them all and now lives inside you. The Christ who left the glory of heaven, who took on flesh, who was laid in the dust of a manger and walked the dusty roads of Galilee, who was nailed to a cross and laid in the dust of a borrowed tomb, and who rose from that dust in a body of glory — that Christ has come to live in you. He entered your dust so that he could carry you to his glory. He became what you are so that you could become like what he is.

So lift up your eyes one last time, and keep them lifted long after this study ends. When the long road wearies you, lift up your eyes: Christ is in you, the hope of glory. When you fail and the dust seems to win the day, lift up your eyes: he is your life, and you will appear with him in glory. When you cannot see how a man like you ever arrives at a glory like that, lift up your eyes to the One who guarantees it from the inside — the indwelling Christ, transforming you degree by degree, who will not quit until the dust is gone and the image is complete. If you miss him, you miss everything. But you have not missed him. He is in you. And he is bringing you home.

This is from dust to glory — the whole road, from a soul clinging to the ground to a man made like Christ, beholding his face. The study is over, but the walk is just beginning. You know the riches now. You know the One who holds them. You know that you are in him and he is in you. So get up off the dust, lift up your eyes, and walk the rest of the road home — Christ in you, the hope of glory, every step of the way.
closingVerse: Your soul once clung to the dust. Lift up your eyes — Christ is in you, the hope of glory, and the road runs all the way home.
carry: Who is one man still clinging to the dust that you will carry this hope to next?
